units.text: Start with the upper-left panel. A Connect attachment uses a supported VPC or Direct Connect attachment as transport. Check that underlying path before investigating the appliance connection layered over it.
Move to the upper right. Connect peers use GRE to carry traffic and BGP to exchange routes. Configure both recommended BGP sessions for each peer to provide routing-plane redundancy.

Inspect the lower-left warning. GRE encapsulation does not itself encrypt traffic. Protect the required transport boundary separately, and verify that the chosen design meets its security requirements.

Return to the full slide and the lower-right peers. Design appliance resilience with multiple peers and routes in both directions. Redundant routing sessions on one peer do not remove every appliance or transport dependency.
Begin with the upper-left checklist. Verify the physical link, virtual interface, BGP session and visible prefixes. Establish which layer works before changing higher-level application policy.
Move to the upper right. Combine VPN tunnel metrics and logs with route tables, flow logs and customer-device counters. Compare evidence from both ends to locate where traffic stops.

Inspect the packet-size example below. Small requests working while large transfers stall can indicate MTU or MSS problems. Test representative packet sizes and account for encapsulation overhead rather than assuming all connectivity is healthy.

With the original full slide visible, test realistic workloads during failover. Record routing convergence, packet loss and application recovery. Success means the complete application path works, including its return traffic and larger transfers.
